title: SenseBERT: Driving Some Sense into BERT
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to make BERT-style language models more sensitive to lexical semantics, especially word sense and WordNet supersenses. The authors argue that standard word-level self-supervision forces the model to infer meaning only indirectly from form, which can leave it weak at disambiguating word senses.

They propose SenseBERT, a modified BERT pretraining approach that adds an auxiliary masked-word supersense prediction objective. The model is trained jointly to predict both the masked word and its WordNet supersense, using weak supervision from WordNet rather than human-annotated sense labels. The architecture also injects supersense information into the input embeddings and changes masking to prioritize words with a single supersense; for out-of-vocabulary words, they test alternative handling strategies.

The empirical evaluation is on NLP benchmark tasks, not education. They test supersense disambiguation on a SemEval-based dataset and the WiC word-in-context task, with additional GLUE results to check general language understanding. SenseBERT improves over vanilla BERT, including strong gains in a frozen-probe setting and state-of-the-art WiC performance for SenseBERTLARGE, while maintaining comparable GLUE performance. The paper provides no teacher, student, or school-related intervention context.

identified_tools.name: SenseBERT
identified_tools.description: A BERT-based language model augmented with weak supervision for predicting WordNet supersenses alongside masked-word prediction, producing a semantic-level language model.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper proposes and evaluates SenseBERT as a pre-trained model, comparing it against vanilla BERT on lexical semantic tasks (SemEval-SS and WiC) and GLUE.

findings.finding_summary: SenseBERT improved supersense disambiguation in the SemEval-SS task relative to BERT. In the frozen-embedding setting, SenseBERTBASE scored 75.6 versus 65.1 for BERTBASE, and SenseBERTLARGE scored 79.5 versus 67.3 for BERTLARGE; in the fine-tuned setting, SenseBERTBASE scored 83.0 versus 79.2 and SenseBERTLARGE scored 83.7 versus 81.1.

SenseBERT improved performance on the Word in Context (WiC) task. SenseBERTBASE scored 70.3 compared with 69.6 for BERTLARGE, and SenseBERTLARGE scored 72.1, which the paper describes as state of the art for this benchmark.

On GLUE, SenseBERTBASE performed on par with BERTBASE overall rather than showing a clear gain or loss. The paper reports an overall score of 77.9 for SenseBERTBASE versus 77.5 for BERTBASE, with mixed task-level differences across the GLUE subtasks.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a model development paper proposing and evaluating a pretraining architecture, not an education study. It does not examine instructional coaching, lesson feedback, teachers, or school context, and it provides no K-12 intervention evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention outcomes are reported, so there is no demonstrated instructional impact to rate. The reported gains are limited to NLP benchmark performance.
